title: Expression Profiling and Overfitting: Training, Testing and Validation
summary: Contrast relative microarray signals with counted SAGE tags, separate class prediction from class discovery, and see why gene-expression classifiers must be validated on data never used to build them.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 79 Hits 1–4 and Traps 1 and 4 (first lesson for Ch. 79). Checked against Simon 2003, McShane 2013 and Liu 2011. Not taught as fact: SAGE tag-size and enzyme details beyond NlaIII/17-bp LongSAGE (BsmFI, 256-bp spacing, microSAGE input), the probe/target naming convention (Hit 3), Human Genome Project figures, WES “~85%”, SELDI/MALDI, the Golub and DLBCL survival figures, 21-/70-gene assay details, HRM and xTAG (no open source read for these).

objectives: Contrast relative (microarray) and counted (SAGE) expression measurement.
Distinguish class prediction (supervised) from class discovery (unsupervised clustering).
Explain overfitting and the validation steps that guard against it.

scenes.title: A perfect signature
scenes.altText: An invented sales sheet: “70-gene tumour signature predicts relapse with 100% accuracy!” Small print: 60 patients; 20,000 genes measured; accuracy calculated on the same 60 patients used to choose the genes. The laboratory director asks: “Should we offer it?” Question token: “What does 100% on the development data really prove?”

cues.text: A company offers a 70-gene tumour signature that predicts relapse with 100 percent accuracy.
The small print: 60 patients, 20,000 genes measured, and the accuracy was calculated on the same 60 patients used to pick the genes.
What does 100 percent on the development data really prove?

props.label: What does 100% on development data prove?

scenes.title: Measuring expression: relative vs counted
scenes.altText: Two schematic panels (Liu 2011). Microarray: pre-designed probes for selected genes on a solid support; hybridization signal measures each gene’s expression RELATIVE to a reference sample. SAGE (serial analysis of gene expression): short sequence tags are cut from each transcript (NlaIII as the anchoring enzyme; 17-bp tags in LongSAGE), sequenced and COUNTED — a direct measurement that needs no reference sample and can detect novel transcripts without prior knowledge of the sequence.

cues.text: There are two classic ways to profile gene expression. A microarray carries pre-designed probes for selected genes.
Labelled sample binds the probes, and the signal tells you each gene’s expression relative to a reference sample, not an absolute count.
Serial analysis of gene expression, or SAGE, cuts a short tag from each transcript, for example with the anchoring enzyme NlaIII, then sequences and counts the tags.
Counting is a direct measurement: no reference sample is needed, and new transcripts can be found without knowing their sequence in advance.

scenes.title: Prediction, discovery, and overfitting
scenes.altText: Goal card (Simon 2003): class PREDICTION — classes are defined in advance, independently of the expression data, and a model learns to assign new samples (supervised); class DISCOVERY — no classes are predefined; cluster analysis groups samples by the distances between their profiles (unsupervised; e.g. Alizadeh 2000 in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma). Cluster analysis is generally not appropriate for class prediction. Overfitting card (McShane 2013; Simon 2003): with far more genes than patients, a model can describe random error or noise instead of the real relationship; including many noise variables reduces accuracy; a model nearly always fits its own development data better than independent data, and many omics predictors fail on a truly independent data set.

cues.text: Expression studies have different goals. In class prediction, the groups, such as relapse or no relapse, are defined in advance, and a supervised model learns to assign new samples.

In class discovery, no groups are defined. Unsupervised cluster analysis looks for new subsets, as was done for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Clustering is not the right tool for building a predictor.
Now the danger. With 20,000 genes and 60 patients, a model can fit random noise instead of the real biology. That is overfitting.
An overfitted model looks excellent on the data used to build it and fails on new patients. Many published omics predictors have failed this way on truly independent data.

scenes.title: How a predictor earns trust
scenes.altText: Bias card (Simon 2003): in a published breast-cancer study, error estimated with gene selection done OUTSIDE the cross-validation loop was 27% (12/44) versus 41% (18/44) when done properly — a seriously biased underestimate from overfitting. McShane 2013: a resubstitution estimate (plugging the development data back in) is biased. Validation card (Simon 2003; McShane 2013): split-sample — a training set builds the model and a separate test set, never used in development, estimates accuracy (e.g. two-thirds training in a lymphoma study); leave-one-out cross-validation repeats the WHOLE model building, including gene selection, with each sample left out in turn; then the predictor, its pre-processing and cut-points are locked down before final validation on independent data. Hook answer: 100% on the development data proves little — require locked-down, independent validation.

cues.text: Testing on the development data hides the problem. In one published study, doing gene selection outside the cross-validation gave a 27 percent error rate; doing it properly gave 41 percent.
The fix is to keep data apart. Build the model on a training set, and estimate accuracy only on a separate test set that played no part in development.
Cross-validation is an alternative, but every step, including choosing the genes, must be repeated with each left-out sample.
Finally, lock down the assay and algorithm, and validate on independent patients. So 100 percent on the development data proves little.

props.title: Keep data apart
lines: Test set never used to build
CV: redo gene selection each fold

props.label: Lock down → validate on independent patients
Hook: 100% on development data proves little

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Microarrays give absolute transcript counts” (✓ relative to a reference sample; SAGE counts tags); “Use cluster analysis to build a relapse predictor” (✓ clustering is for class discovery; prediction uses supervised methods with predefined classes); “100% accuracy on the development set means the test is ready” (✓ resubstitution estimates are biased — independent validation of a locked-down predictor is required).

cues.text: Trap one: microarrays give absolute transcript counts. No: they measure expression relative to a reference. SAGE counts tags.
Trap two: use cluster analysis to build a relapse predictor. No: clustering is for class discovery; prediction needs supervised methods and predefined classes.
Trap three: 100 percent accuracy on the development set means the test is ready. No: that estimate is biased. Lock it down and validate on independent patients.

props.title: ✗ “Microarrays give absolute counts.”
lines: ✓ Relative to reference · SAGE counts tags

scenes.title: The test set never sees training
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Studying from the answer key: a student who memorizes this year’s exam scores 100% on it and fails next year’s. The test set must never see training — not even to pick the genes.” Tokens: Train → Test → Lock → Independent. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: an overfitted model is a student who memorized this year’s exam. Perfect on that paper, lost on next year’s. The test set must never see training, not even to choose the genes.

Where it breaks: a model can also fail for real biological or technical reasons, like a different patient population or assay drift, even when the statistics were done properly; and cross-validation within one cohort is still not independent validation.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Microarray = relative to reference · SAGE = counted tags · prediction = supervised · discovery = clustering”, “Genes ≫ patients → overfitting: never test on training data; lock down, then validate on independent patients”.

cues.text: With thousands of genes and few patients a classifier can fit noise, so its accuracy must come from samples never used to build it, ideally from independent patients after the predictor is locked down.

props.label: Array relative · SAGE counted · prediction supervised · discovery clusters
Genes ≫ patients → overfitting: lock down, validate independently

explanation.what: Plain language: when a test uses thousands of genes but only a few dozen patients, it can “learn” chance patterns, so its accuracy must be checked on patients it has never seen. Scientific terms: microarray, reference sample, SAGE, tag counting, class prediction, class discovery, supervised and unsupervised methods, cluster analysis, overfitting, noise variables, resubstitution, split-sample validation, leave-one-out cross-validation, locked-down predictor, independent validation.
explanation.why: Each extra gene is another chance to match random noise in a small sample. Testing on the same data used to select genes and fit the model rewards that noise; only data kept completely apart reveals how the model will perform on future patients.
explanation.measure: Microarray: expression relative to a reference; SAGE: counted tags (Liu 2011). Accuracy: split-sample training/test or cross-validation with gene selection repeated in each loop (Simon 2003); lock down and validate on independent data (McShane 2013). Example: improper CV 27% vs proper 41% error (Simon 2003).
explanation.differs: Class prediction (predefined classes, supervised) vs class discovery (no predefined classes, clustering); resubstitution or improper CV (biased) vs split-sample/proper CV and independent validation.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: recognize overfitting from a small-sample, many-gene story; choose supervised vs unsupervised methods; know microarrays are relative while SAGE counts.

comparisons.title: Class prediction vs class discovery
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether class labels are used to build the model.

comparisons.title: Microarray vs SAGE
comparisons.distinguisher: Relative hybridization signal vs direct tag counts.

mnemonic.text: Studying from the answer key: a student who memorizes this year’s exam scores 100% on it and fails next year’s. The test set must never see training — not even to pick the genes.
mnemonic.explanation: Overfitting rewards memorized noise; only unseen data shows true performance.
mnemonic.limitation: Models also fail from population or assay changes; cross-validation in one cohort is not independent validation; overfitting is statistical, not literal memorization.

The 27% vs 41% example is from one published study.

questions.stem: A 40-gene classifier built from 50 patients is 98% accurate when re-applied to those same 50 patients but 60% accurate in a new hospital. What best explains this?

options.text: Overfitting to noise in the small development set
options.rationale: Correct. With many genes and few patients the model fit chance patterns; resubstitution accuracy is biased.

options.text: The new hospital used class discovery
options.rationale: Incorrect. The model is a class predictor; the drop reflects overfitting, not the analysis type at the new site.

options.text: Microarrays give absolute counts that vary by hospital
options.rationale: Incorrect. Microarrays measure relative expression, and the core problem is the biased development estimate.
Incorrect. Adding noise variables generally reduces prediction accuracy.

questions.stem: Investigators want to know whether tumours with identical microscopic appearance fall into previously unrecognized molecular groups. Which approach fits?

options.rationale: Correct. No classes are predefined; clustering groups samples by profile similarity.

options.text: A supervised classifier trained on known outcomes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Supervised methods need predefined classes; this is class prediction.
Incorrect. Cross-validation estimates prediction accuracy; it does not discover groups.
Incorrect. Resubstitution is a (biased) way to estimate accuracy, not a discovery method.

questions.stem: During leave-one-out cross-validation of a gene-expression predictor, when should the genes be selected?

options.text: Afresh within each loop, using only the samples left in the training set
options.rationale: Correct. Simon 2003: the whole model, including gene selection, is rebuilt each time; selecting genes beforehand biases error estimates.

options.text: Once, using all samples, before cross-validation starts
options.rationale: Incorrect. This lets the left-out samples influence the model; in one study it gave 27% vs a proper 41% error.

options.text: After testing, choosing the genes that predicted best
options.rationale: Incorrect. Choosing genes after seeing test results is overfitting to the test set.

options.text: Gene selection is unnecessary in cross-validation
options.rationale: Incorrect. Selection is part of model building and must be repeated in each loop.
